title: What are the pros of having a Junior level in C# to do Unity Games with Astra?
author: ElioVibe
selftext: Very concretely, do you have exemples of what edge it brings?

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
faster debugging, an idea of software development principles so you know things like, "dont make everything global variables" or that packages exist you can use to extend functions/classes without having the AI reinvent the wheel, stuff like that. 

  
No concrete examples though, sorry.

comments.author: Cubey42
comments.body: Having knowledge is better because you can be more specific about important things. AI will often take the easiest way out of doing something. I have little to no coding experience and I haven't run into any obstacles I couldn't work through.

replies.author: ElioVibe
replies.body: It doesn't limit you?  I think there's a reason why all the games here have a super basic gameplay with bad physics

replies.author: Cubey42
replies.body:
It's not to say there isn't any challenges. Most of what's here is people maybe trying things for the first time. You usually aren't going to find any polish in the one-shots in short projects people have made here, no different than anyone's first sketchbook. You can be in as much control or as little control as you want to be. 

Think about it like a tool for a sculptor. The one shots that people do is the equivalent of trying to make the statue of David with just a single cut. Yeah it might look like the statue of David but it's probably going to have imperfections and less than ideal composition. But a person who makes many cuts over time will make a much better version, and someone who's very gifted and makes many cuts will still make a statue of David worth remembering.

replies.author: ElioVibe
replies.body: I'm not talking simply about the one shots, even games here that are developped for month seem basic and limited

replies.author: Cubey42
replies.body: Well yeah, a month really isn't alot of time. I'm at 9 months and I still haven't shown mine.

replies.author: Kosh_Ascadian
replies.body:
Yes, if you don't know game design and at least basic game programming/architecture your project will always be limited (at current AI capabilities).

Your intuition on this is correct.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
That's a design issue, not a code issue.  Most people here are either trying to churn slop for a quick buck (the asset flip crowd) or simply know nothing about *design* beyond "I thought this one game I played once was fun"

Which to be fair, is the same in the non-AI indie dev subs

replies.author: Kosh_Ascadian
replies.body:
It can be an issue with both/either.

I remember a post here on how someone put in multiple thousands of dollars for a very basic looking 3/4 top down view world with basic x-y movement. After thousands of dollars and weeks (or was it months) of work the game couldn't even get basic depth layering correct. And all the prompting of "fix it please" wasn't doing anything.

Ie "depth = -y" was unknown technology to the dev.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Its semantic at this point, but id argue that that's still design.  "These things should layer in exactly this way, and interact in this way" is design, the AI simply failed to implement that because the design intent was not clearly conveyed (and as such, likely repeatedly *incorrectly* conveyed).

Sure, the implementation is "depth = -y" but if the person prompting the AI has no concept of asset layers or depth, the machine is only coding what it was actually told to code.

replies.author: Kosh_Ascadian
replies.body:
I'd separate it because it's not game design knowledge. It's game project architecture/design/systems/coding knowledge.

I don't really care what you call it, but you need skills and know-how in it to do a good job.

And even though I'm fine calling it design know-how if you want since I hate semantic arguments... I would still argue that if you take a "game design course" somewhere or something you wont learn this and similar stuff.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
For sure.  I think the important takeaway is really that "design" is just a lot more than being an "idea guy" and actually requires technical accumen to bridge the gap between the idea, the tangible "how and why" of gameplay, and the technical structure of implementation.

Which these typical posts just don't have, whatever we want to call it :p
